1:
Who is speaking they supply from the chapter before. Gill points back to the glorious Person on the throne just described; Wesley names him outright as Christ; Ellicott declines to name him but reasons that the unexplained He, in connection with that vision, could be none other than the Most High whose glory it revealed, and marks a change in kind: this voice was articulate, speaking in words the man could understand.

The title carries most of the weight, divided between humility and idiom. Henry takes it as a humble diminishing title, lest the man be lifted up with the abundance of the revelations: among the living creatures he must remember that he is himself a dying one, and God, with a retinue of angels about the throne ready to go on his errands, passed them by and pitched on a son of man, so that the treasure is in earthen vessels and the messenger's terror does not make us afraid. Ellicott makes it a fact of language: the phrase is common in Scripture for man, but is never used in addressing a prophet except here and once to one other, and here above ninety times, because the prophet of the captivity was addressed in the common terms of the country he lived in, the usage being so ordinary in the Aramaic tongues that one version applies it to Adam himself. Wesley counts ninety-five at least, and for Henry's reason, to keep humble a man with such great revelations.

Calvin reads the raising as a doctrine about two kinds of fear. God never prostrates his people so as to leave them lying on the earth, but raises them afterwards, whereas the reprobate are so frightened at the sight of God that they fall and never rise; the impious dread his voice, are terrified by his hand when signs of wrath appear, and yet remain lifeless. In the faithful the pride of the flesh is corrected, and then the hand is stretched out and they are restored as from death to life.

Calvin then makes the sequence itself the lesson. Nothing was accomplished by the voice until the Spirit was added: God works efficiently by his words, but the efficacy is not in the words themselves and proceeds from the secret instinct of the Spirit, the work of the Spirit joined to the word and yet distinguishable from it. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion another way, listing occasions when divine strength was vouchsafed to prophets overcome by their visions, and concluding that the spirit here is no mere human vigour of the man's own.

What that spirit is divides Gill and Clarke exactly. Gill rules out two candidates: the man's own soul, which does not appear to have gone out of him, and a ministering angel, angels being never said to enter into the prophets or the people of God. It is the Holy Spirit, and the same Spirit that was in the living creatures and in the wheels, in the ministers and in the churches. Clarke says the opposite in a line: this spirit was different from the one by which the wheels were moved, the spirit of prophecy, whose office was not merely to enable a man to foretell but to purify and refine his heart. Wesley settles it with Gill, the same spirit that actuated the living creatures.

Two smaller points close the passage. Clarke reads the standing as service, that he might stand as a servant before his master to receive orders, and then objects to the chapter division: either the preceding chapter should have ended a verse earlier, or this verse belongs to it and the next should open the chapter. Ellicott warns against reading it too physically, since all these things still take place within the vision, the man now instructed by a direct voice while the sight remained before him.
3:
Clarke traces the title through three stages: given first to this prophet, then to the other who saw visions in exile, and after that to the Man Christ Jesus; to the prophets to remind them of their frailty and keep them of one nature with those they were sent to, to the third to show that one whose acts demonstrated him God was also really man.

Ellicott settles who is meant by Israel and then turns the other word against them. After the captivity of the ten tribes the two remaining, with such others as had joined them, are constantly called Israel, the continuity of the nation reckoned preserved in the remnant; only where the two parts must be distinguished is Israel set against Judah. Then the epithet: the word rendered nation is literally a plural, the one commonly used for the heathen, so that the children of Israel are here called rebellious heathen, no epithet carrying home more forcibly the antagonism they stood in. And yet the God they had turned from was sending them a prophet still, answering the bow in the cloud about the majesty on high.

Hardness of face they take up together. Gill glosses it as we say a man is brazen faced: a forehead refusing to be ashamed, faces harder than rock, sin declared openly and not hidden. Ellicott notes the epithet returns later, its answer being the prophet's own face made strong and his forehead harder than flint. Calvin sets face beside heart: hypocrisy often lies hid in the mind, and men swelling with malice do not betray what they nourish, whereas these opposed God without disguise, in their very countenances, like horned oxen or furious bulls.

The messenger formula draws Clarke into a warning to preachers. Let them know that what is declared is the Lord's message, that they may receive it with reverence; and let no preacher suppose that because a thing agrees with his own creed it is God's word, since endless false doctrines are foisted on the world that way. Bring the creed to the word first and try whether it is right; that done, leave it where you please and warn men from what is recorded there. Ellicott stops at the name instead: the Lord God of the English is the Lord Jehovah of the original, the second name taking the pointing of the first and so translated God.

Whether they hear or forbear draws four consolations. Gill takes the second word as ceasing, from hearing on one reading and from sinning on another, and tells the prophet not to be discouraged if the ministry is fruitless. Clarke gets two certainties out of it: God in mercy had given due warning, and they were inexcusable for not taking it. Calvin makes it a rule for despondency: when we do not succeed as we wish we are inclined to despair, but God has another object besides the salvation of men, the removal of every pretext for error, since hypocrites think themselves excusable unless God affords them the light of his doctrine. Ellicott divides the effect instead: the word cannot return void, but its character depends on those it comes to, a savour of death to one and of life to another, so that some by the river would be brought back and become the remnant while others would be made more obdurate; neither could remain as before.

Calvin closes on sign and word. Figures are illusory without an explanation: had the vision only been offered to the eye and no voice followed, what would the advantage have been? Only when God confirmed the vision by his word could the man say with profit that he had seen the glory of God. The same holds of the sacraments: signs presented to the eyes alone are dead images until the word throws life into them.
6:
Ellicott settles the two words first. They occur nowhere else, though their sense is plain; the first might admit the marginal rendering rebels, but both should be taken together, and as nouns rather than adjectives, which agrees better with the scorpions that follow and with the strongly figurative manner of the book.

Henry works the figure hard. Briers and thorns scratch and tear and vex a man whichever way he turns, and are the fruit of sin and the curse, of equal date with the enmity between the two seeds; wicked men are hurtful to the ground, choke the good seed, hinder God's husbandry, and are nigh unto cursing with their end to be burned. Wesley adds that briers run up among thorns, a fit emblem of the frowardness of sinners.

The scorpion is a step up, and Henry marks the distance: its sting is a thousand times more hurtful than a brier's scratch, and persecutors are of the serpent's seed, more subtle than any beast of the field. What makes it worse is the address: the man dwells among them and is not safe in his own house, and God notices it as the Lord noticed of one of the churches that it dwelt where Satan's seat is. Henry closes on the contrast: he had been conversing with angels in vision, and coming down from that mount he finds he lives among scorpions.

On the looks and the words they converge, and Henry adds a historical note. Gill has the greatest among them, princes and nobles whose grandeur and stern looks and big words might awe a man. Wesley makes the words accusations, threats, or whatever a malicious heart can suggest to the tongue. Henry has them hector and look scornfully, doing their utmost to face him down and put him out of countenance, so as to drive him off from prophesying, or failing that to disturb the repose of his mind; and he notes why it went no further, that they were now themselves in subjection and divested of all power, so that looks and words were the only persecution left them.

Calvin will not take the words as mere threats. They are calumnies: hypocrites rise up with great confidence, complain of the injury done them, and presumptuously take the name of God upon themselves; the adversaries of his own day, he says, not only vomit out threats but boast themselves to be the Church, confirm it by a perpetual succession, and argue that the Church is never without the Holy Spirit. He makes the repetition count: God says once, and then twice, that we are not to fear such men's words, and since he allows us to despise that language there is no reason to be daunted when they thunder out the name of the Church with inflated cheeks. He stops at the second verb as well, which means to be rubbed and broken and is transferred to the mind, so that the charge is not to be broken in spirit; and none, he concludes, are fit for the office but those armed with fortitude, who do not vacillate under unjust calumny, as the apostle persevered through evil report and good.

The second verse repeats the first, read as a rule for fruitless work. Clarke says to declare it whether they receive it or persecute him for it, that they may be without excuse. Calvin allows hope its place but insists the result be left with God: even if you sing a song to the deaf, as the proverb has it, you shall not cease to utter his words, and one called to teach must not regard the conduct of mankind. Wesley closes with a sentence he takes over almost verbatim from Henry, that they who will do anything to purpose in the service of God must not fear the faces of men.
8:
Eating the word they take figuratively and press differently. Clarke makes it dietary: take the word as thou wouldst take thy proper food, that it may strengthen the soul as nourishment does the body; and hearers should so hear it read, mark, learn and inwardly digest it. Ellicott keeps it inside the vision, as with the book eaten by the seer of the later revelation. Gill draws the order of ministry from it: the words were not his own but the Lord's, so he must hear before he spoke.

Calvin agrees that no one can discharge the teacher's office who is not first a proficient in God's school, and names the stumbling-block the charge removes: a multitude has great power to disturb us, the consent of a whole people being a tempest in which even those not wicked are carried along. And the people in question boasted itself divinely elected and bore the symbol of its adoption in the flesh, which lets him turn again on the adversaries of his own century.

Whose hand it was they answer three ways. Gill says not an angel's but Christ's own, and not a real hand but the likeness of one. Ellicott corrects the rendering to was put forth rather than was sent: no hand by itself carrying a roll was despatched, but a hand was stretched out to him, either a cherub's or one from the throne above, as in the corresponding later vision an angel hands the book over. Clarke leaves the owner alone, taking the hand for an emblem of divine power. Calvin finds the certainty in it: a volume merely presented might have been doubted, but one held out by a hand visibly sent from God leaves nothing wanting.

The roll turns three of them into antiquarians. Clarke observes that all ancient books were written to be rolled, whence volume comes from the verb to roll; Calvin gives the same etymology and adds that the archives of princes hold nothing ancient that is not on rolls. Wesley describes parchment written along its length, piece fastened to piece until the whole would hold what was to be written, then wrapped about a rod.

Writing on both sides is the anomaly, and each accounts for it. Ellicott says rolls were ordinarily written on one side only, the other being inconvenient to read, and takes the exception as denoting the fullness of the message. Clarke testifies from his own shelves: several Hebrew rolls lie before him, all written on the inside only, of vellum or half-tanned sheep and goat skin sewed together, running to several yards, with a Sanskrit roll of sixty feet also written only within, and a Koran two inches broad and twelve feet long, weighing half an ounce. His explanation is practical: the prophecy was long and all to one effect, so that they might see the mind of God wherever they looked. Wesley says only, on the side inward when rolled and on the outward side too.

The contents are three words, and they weigh them. Clarke calls it an awful assemblage: lamentation on all hands, a groan from the dying, alas from the survivors; and he sets against it the mercy of glad tidings. Calvin says the middle word can mean meditation or speech simply, but joined with lamentations it must be a mournful strain: the instruction was not sweet but full of sorrow, the man a herald denouncing war with no message of peace. He also hears length in them, not a brief errand but much time imposed, lest after three or four speeches the hearers ask whether that was not enough. Ellicott bounds it the other way: this was the message's whole character only until the judgment fell, after which the prophecies turn consolatory. Gill takes the spreading as instruction: it was unrolled that he might understand before he delivered.
